title: St Lucie Cherry: Ancient Cherries You Can Visit
meta_description: Usually a shrub, six metres at most, except Budapest's 250-year-old, 11.2-metre specimen. Three St Lucie cherries mapped, Budapest to Den Bosch.
intro: Prunus mahaleb is usually a shrub, six metres tall on a good day, grown mostly as rootstock for other cherries rather than as a specimen in its own right. Three trees on this site ignore that description entirely. Budapest's, in the ELTE Fuveszkert botanical garden, stands 11.2 metres tall with a trunk 339 centimetres round, already growing on a nobleman's private estate before the university bought the ground around it in 1847. Den Bosch's, rooted for roughly a century against the medieval city wall on Parklaan, was nominated for the Dutch national Bomen Top 50 in 2022. Matera's, the thinnest evidenced of the three, has given its name to the city's Lanera district even though this pass could not confirm whether it still stands. Hungarians call the species sajmeggy, the Dutch call it Weichselboom; both names describe a fruit few gardeners plant a tree this size to get.
